claims.source: We also included UM171, which improves the maintenance of HSC functional capacity (Fares et al., 2014) and can improve transduction efficiency in these cells (Ngom et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The results section cites published literature (Ngom et al., 2018) to support this claim about UM171 effects on transduction.

claims.claim: At lower RNP concentrations, there was a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer.
claims.source: At lower RNP concentrations, we observed a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer, though this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR = 0.02 and FDR = 0.48, respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR values) to support this claim.

claims.claim: Increasing RNP concentration showed a benefit to overall editing efficiency.
claims.source: Similarly, increasing RNP concentration also showed a benefit to overall editing efficiency (FDR = 0.08, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) to support this claim.

claims.claim: Both the addition of an electroporation enhancer and the increase in RNP concentration resulted in significantly decreased cell numbers indicating toxicity.
claims.source: Both the addition of an electroporation enhancer and the increase in RNP concentration, however, resulted in significantly decreased cell numbers indicating toxicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data showing decreased cell numbers to support this toxicity claim.

claims.claim: A nested PCR was required to avoid non-specific amplification from non-integrated AAV donors.
claims.source: One critical factor we discovered here was that for this assessment a nested PCR was required with outer primers outside the homology arms of the AAV, as otherwise non-specific amplification from non-integrated donors predominated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A demonstrating the need for nested PCR.

claims.claim: The BspEI-based assay is accurate down to ~1% integration efficiency.
claims.source: Using defined mixtures of WT and BspEI DNA, we show that this assay is accurate down to ~1% integration efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B demonstrating assay accuracy.

claims.claim: For AAV, a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 400 MOI gave the highest integration rate prior to observable toxicity with an integration rate of 19.8%.
claims.source: For AAV, a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 400 MOI gave the highest integration rate prior to observable toxicity with an integration rate of 19.8% (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1C and D to support this claim about optimal AAV MOI.

claims.claim: Short ssODN donors showed an integration rate of 12% at 50 pmol.
claims.source: For these, 100 ng of amplified DNA was added to 1 x NEBuffer 3.1 with 2 U BspEI. These were then incubated at 37 °C for 1 hr and then run on a 2% TAE agarose gel with GelRed and quantified by densitometry. For AAV donors, these were run directly on a gel, and integration quantified based on the size shift from the introduced 143 bp synthetic intron. Finally, for ssODN with silent mutations, PCR products were purified by GeneJet PCR purification, quantified by nanodrop, and 5–15 ng sent for Sanger sequencing at the IRIC Genomics core with the primer pri0003-A1 (Key Resource Table). Integration was then quantified using ICE Analysis (Synthego Performance Analysis, 2019. v3.0. Synthego) with a comparison between each edited sample back to a matched unedited control.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E to support this claim about ssODN integration rate.

claims.claim: Toxicity for both ssODN donors was independent of the presence of the Cas9 nuclease.
claims.source: Interestingly, toxicity for both ssODN donors was independent of the presence of the Cas9 nuclease (equivalent in the no RNP condition), suggesting that it is likely an innate immune reaction to the single-stranded DNA rather than the editing process itself.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1F and provides an interpretation based on the observation.

claims.claim: An increased HDR efficiency up to 70% was observed with M3814.
claims.source: We observed an increased HDR efficiency up to 70% with M3814 (Figure 2A), equivalent to reports with inhibition of 53BP1 (De Ravin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2A to support this claim about M3814 effects.

claims.claim: AZD7648 has been reported to inhibit DNA-PK with reduced off-target activity on PI3K.
claims.source: We also tested another DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648 which has been reported to inhibit DNA-PK with reduced off-target activity on PI3K (Fok et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The results section cites published literature (Fok et al., 2019) to support this claim about AZD7648 specificity.

claims.claim: Improved editing efficiency was observed at 0.5 µM with AZD7648 compared to M3814.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed improved editing efficiency at 0.5 µM with AZD7648 compared to M3814, and 0.5 µM AZD7648 was equivalent to 5 µM M3814 (Figure 2A, FDR = 0.01 and FDR = 0.24, respectively).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR values) in Figure 2A to support this claim.

claims.claim: Toxicity was marginally but statistically significantly lower for AZD7648 compared to M3814 at 0.5 µM.
claims.source: Toxicity, as assessed by viable cell counts, was also marginally but statistically significantly lower for AZD7648 compared to M3814 at 0.5 µM (Figure 2B, FDR = 0.02 for 0.5 µM).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) in Figure 2B to support this claim.

claims.claim: The addition of RS1 either alone or together with AZD7648 was detrimental to editing efficiency and toxic to cells.
claims.source: In this context, the addition of RS1 either alone or together with AZD7648 was detrimental to editing efficiency and toxic to cells (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2C to support this claim about RS1 effects.

claims.claim: The combination of p53siRNA and AZD7648 was able to achieve mean efficiencies of 80% and up to 96%.
claims.source: The combination of p53siRNA and AZD7648, however, was able to achieve mean efficiencies of 80% and up to 96% in these tests with minimal toxicity (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2C and D to support this claim about combined effects.

claims.claim: The number of conditions tested in each experiment was related to editing efficiency.
claims.source: A closer examination of experimental factors that may affect efficiency revealed this to be related to the number of conditions tested in each experiment (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2E showing a correlation between condition number and efficiency.

claims.claim: There are likely technical factors associated with cell handling and nucleofection timing that play an important role in overall efficiency.
claims.source: This suggests that there are likely technical factors associated with cell handling and nucleofection timing that play an important role in overall efficiency.
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the observed correlation between condition number and efficiency.

claims.claim: A mean efficiency of 97% with AAV donors was observed in tests performed with no more than four simultaneous conditions at nucleofection.
claims.source: Confirming our observed negative correlation between condition number and efficiency, in these tests performed with no more than four simultaneous conditions at nucleofection, we observed a mean efficiency of 97% with AAV donors (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about AAV efficiency.

claims.claim: The incorporation of additional spacer-breaking mutations drastically improved editing efficiency up to 94% for ssODN donors.
claims.source: Interestingly, the incorporation of these additional spacer-breaking mutations drastically improved editing efficiency up to 94%, nearly that of the AAV (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about spacer mutation effects.

claims.claim: The design incorporating only the silent spacer mutations, but no PAM mutation achieved a mean efficiency of 84%.
claims.source: Surprisingly, even the design incorporating only the silent spacer mutations, but no PAM mutation achieved a mean efficiency of 84%, further highlighting the importance of spacer mutations in donor design.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about silent mutation effects.

claims.claim: No detectable edits were found at the top 3 predicted off-target sites either with or without AZD7648.
claims.source: Analysis of the top 3 predicted off-target sites in 3 sets of samples revealed no detectable edits at these sites either with or without AZD7648 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2H and supplements to support this claim about off-target editing.

claims.claim: Off-target editing at predicted sites is not affected by AZD7648 addition, at least with well-designed gRNA.
claims.source: This suggests that off-target editing at predicted sites is not affected by AZD7648 addition, at least with well-designed gRNA.
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the off-target analysis data.

claims.claim: No significant differences in editing efficiencies from bulk measurements were observed regardless of sub-population.
claims.source: We observed no significant differences in editing efficiencies from bulk measurements regardless of sub-population suggesting that the editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3A to support this claim about editing across the hierarchy.

claims.claim: A slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of CD34+ cells of the advanced progenitor phenotype.
claims.source: We also observed a generally equivalent representation of each population within the CD34 compartment between silent edited and control cells, though a slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of CD34 + cells of the advanced progenitor phenotype (FDR = 0.007; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) in Figure 3B to support this claim.

claims.claim: A slight drop in colony number was observed even without editing, consistent with donor-induced toxicity.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier observations that donor alone induced some toxicity, we observed a slight drop in colony number even without editing (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3D and relates it to earlier observations.

claims.claim: Colony number was further decreased with editing.
claims.source: Colony number was further decreased with editing (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3D to support this claim about editing effects on colony number.

claims.claim: No changes to colony type were observed with editing.
claims.source: Importantly, however, no changes to colony type were observed (Figure 3E), suggesting that while there is a quantitative drop in progenitor function, this was even across progenitor types and the capability of remaining cells was not affected.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3E to support this claim about colony type distribution.

claims.claim: Colonies showed a preponderance of homozygous edits.
claims.source: Analysis of the editing on colonies revealed editing across most colonies with a predominance of homozygous edits (Figure 3F), as expected by our high editing efficiencies.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3F to support this claim about zygosity in colonies.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the frequency of highly proliferative clones between edited cells and non-edited controls.
claims.source: Critically, there was no significant difference in the frequency of highly proliferative clones between edited cells and non-edited controls (Figure 3I), suggesting that the editing process does not substantially affect the most regenerative subset of HSC.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3I with statistical analysis to support this claim about LTC-IC frequency.

claims.claim: There was a trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation and transient clones in the edited condition.
claims.source: While there was not a significant difference, there was a trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation and transient clones in the edited condition (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3I showing a non-significant trend.

claims.claim: A highly significant monotonic decrease in mutant allele frequency was observed with increasing silent donor proportion.
claims.source: At 48 hr post editing a bulk sample was harvested to determine overall editing efficiency. This showed a highly significant monotonic decrease in mutant allele frequency with increasing silent donor proportion (p<<0.001, Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis in Figure 4B to support this claim about tunable zygosity.

claims.claim: No significant differences in clonogenic efficiency were observed across conditions in the zygosity tuning experiments.
claims.source: No significant differences in clonogenic efficiency were observed across conditions though there were no large clones (i.e. in excess of 100 cells) in the 100% mutant donor condition (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 4C to support this claim about clonogenic efficiency.

claims.claim: A preponderance of homozygous edits was observed with all mutant donors, with a progressive increase in heterozygous or homozygous silent as the proportion of silent donor was increased.
claims.source: As expected, we observed a preponderance of homozygous edits with all mutant donors, with a progressive increase in heterozygous or homozygous silent as the proportion of silent donor was increased (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 4D to support this claim about zygosity distribution.

claims.claim: AZD7648 is optimal for improving HDR efficiency in HSPCs, consistent with demonstrations of its improved potency and specificity.
claims.source: Through these tests, we confirmed reports that DNA-PK inhibition was an effective method to improve HDR efficiency (De Ravin et al., 2021; Shy et al., 2023), and identified AZD7648 to be optimal for this task, consistent with demonstrations of its improved potency and specificity (Fok et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Fok et al., 2019) and relates it to the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence were necessary to achieve maximal efficiencies with ssODN donors.
claims.source: The difference is likely attributable to the design of the ssODN donors themselves, as we also found that additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence were necessary to achieve maximal efficiencies.
claims.evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation based on the experimental findings comparing ssODN designs.

claims.claim: Most AAV donors insert a tag of some description, providing a spacer disruption built-in to these systems.
claims.source: Given that most AAV donors insert a tag of some description (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2022; De Ravin et al., 2021), such a spacer disruption has been built-in to these systems, but not in the competing ssODN.
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2022; De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about AAV donor design.

claims.claim: The number of conditions simultaneously processed at the time of nucleofection had a substantial effect on efficiency.
claims.source: One surprising factor that had a substantial effect on efficiency was the number of conditions simultaneously processed at the time of nucleofection.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental finding about condition number effects.

claims.claim: The effect of condition number on efficiency likely corresponds to the handling time.
claims.source: This likely corresponds to the handling time, and may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection previously reported (Charlesworth et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation and cites published literature (Charlesworth et al., 2018) to support this inference.

claims.claim: Editing did not change the frequency of populations across the hematopoietic hierarchy.
claims.source: To ensure that the editing process was functional throughout the hierarchy, and not specifically toxic to specific levels, we demonstrated that editing did not change the frequency of populations across this hierarchy and that editing efficiency was equivalent throughout, including in the HSC phenotype.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about editing across the hierarchy.

claims.claim: Editing did not alter the distribution of myeloid outputs in clonogenic assays.
claims.source: Beyond this, using clonogenic assays for progenitor differentiation, we demonstrated that editing did not alter the distribution of myeloid outputs.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about myeloid differentiation.

claims.claim: Previous reports demonstrated that editing rates were consistent in pre-transplant measured and post-transplantation both with and without DNA-PK inhibition.
claims.source: These findings together with previous reports demonstrating that editing rates were consistent in pre-transplant measured and post-transplantation both with and without DNA-PK inhibition (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) suggest that the reported editing protocol also edited cells capable of engrafting a mouse for >6 months (functional long-term HSC).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about editing consistency.

claims.claim: A modest decrease in CFC potential was observed with editing.
claims.source: We did, however, observe a modest decrease in CFC potential and a non-significant trend towards the same in low proliferation LTC-IC, suggesting that late progenitors may be more sensitive to the editing process than the most primitive.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about CFC and LTC-IC effects.

claims.claim: Much of the toxicity both in direct cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery, regardless of editing.
claims.source: It is important to note, however, that our and others' data suggest that remaining CFCs appear to retain normal function (Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021). Interestingly, much of the toxicity both in direct cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery, regardless of editing.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings and cites published literature (Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) about toxicity sources.

claims.claim: Toxicity is likely mediated by innate immune responses to DNA.
claims.source: This suggests that toxicity is likely mediated by innate immune responses to DNA (Piras and Kajaste-Rudnitski, 2021).
claims.evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation and cites published literature (Piras and Kajaste-Rudnitski, 2021) to support this inference.

claims.claim: No off-target edits were observed at predicted sites, regardless of whether edits were done in the presence of AZD7648/p53 siRNA or not.
claims.source: We did not observe any off-target edits at predicted sites, regardless of whether edits were done in the presence of AZD7648/p53 siRNA or not, suggesting that the protocol presented here did not substantially increase off-target editing frequencies.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about off-target editing.

claims.claim: No increases in off target editing or large-scale genomic rearrangements were observed when donor was present with 53BP1 inhibition.
claims.source: This was consistent with findings from other studies using 53BP1 inhibition which similarly targets NHEJ, where they observed no increases in off target editing or large-scale genomic rearrangements were observed when donor was present (De Ravin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about safety with NHEJ inhibition.

claims.claim: Another manuscript showed similar effects for the addition of AZD7648 as being able to increase the precise editing efficiency of human HSPCs.
claims.source: During the time that this article was undergoing its publication process, another manuscript came out showing similar effects for the addition of AZD7648 as being able to increase the precise editing efficiency of human HSPCs (as well as T and B cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells) (Selvaraj et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to support this claim about AZD7648 effects in other studies.

claims.claim: The other manuscript showed an increase in efficiency to similar levels using AAV6 donors.
claims.source: In their manuscript they also show an increase in efficiency to similar levels using AAV6 donors, and similar but slightly lower inefficiencies that we achieved in ssODN donors (Selvaraj et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings.

claims.claim: The differences in ssODN efficiency are likely attributable to the use of shorter ssODN donors and choice of silent spacer disrupting mutations.
claims.source: The differences are likely attributable to our use of shorter ssODN donors and our choice of silent spacer disrupting mutations in them.
claims.evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation comparing the current study to another published work.

claims.claim: Both ssODN donor length and silent spacer disrupting mutations have been previously shown to impact the integration efficiency.
claims.source: Both of these factors have been previously shown to impact the integration efficiency (Okamoto et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Okamoto et al., 2019) to support this claim about factors affecting integration.

claims.claim: Similar viability effects of AAV donor and lack of negative effects from 0.5 µM AZD7648 were observed in another study.
claims.source: We also observed similar viability effects of AAV donor, and lack of negative effects from 0.5 µM AZD7648 (Selvaraj et al., 2024), though we extend this with the effects of the ssODN donors and ssODN donor length on viability.
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings about viability.

claims.claim: Another study similarly showed that CFC distributions are not affected by the editing process.
claims.source: Again, we similarly show that CFC distributions are not affected by the editing process (Selvaraj et al., 2024), though we again extend this with information on the effect of ssODN donors on total CFC frequency.
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings about CFC distributions.

claims.claim: Another article used AZD7648 together with Polθ inhibitors in several non-hematopoietic cell lines to improve editing efficiency.
claims.source: Finally, another article was also published while we were in our review process in which they used AZD7648 together with Polθ inhibitors in several non-hematopoietic cell lines to improve editing efficiency (Wimberger et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Wimberger et al., 2023) to reference related work.

claims.claim: The P95H mutation in SRSF2 is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and clonal hematopoiesis.
claims.source: Of note, the PAM mutation in our mutant donors introduces a P95H mutation which is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and clonal hematopoiesis (Watson et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2011; van der Werf et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The results section cites published literature (Watson et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2011; van der Werf et al., 2021) to support this claim about the P95H mutation.

claims.claim: Clones with high proliferative potential at 8 weeks in the LTC-IC assay correlate with those HSC with the highest regenerative potential in vivo.
claims.source: We have previously shown that clones with high proliferative potential at 8 weeks in this assay correlate with those HSC with the highest regenerative potential in vivo (Knapp et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The results section cites the authors' previous work (Knapp et al., 2018) to support this claim about LTC-IC assay predictive value.

claims.claim: Phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells.
claims.source: While phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019), not all of these markers are stable on cultured cells.
claims.evidence: The results section cites published literature (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019) to support this claim about CD49f marker selectivity.

claims.claim: Cell density was maintained below 250,000 cells/mL of total media to prevent auto-inhibition of the primitive cells.
claims.source: Cell density was maintained below 250,000 cells/mL of total media to prevent auto-inhibition of the primitive cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Csaszar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The methods section cites published literature (Knapp et al., 2017; Csaszar et al., 2012) to support this culture condition.

claims.claim: At lower RNP concentrations, the electroporation enhancer benefit was not present at higher concentrations.
claims.source: At lower RNP concentrations, we observed a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer, though this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR = 0.02 and FDR = 0.48, respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis to support this claim about concentration-dependent effects.

claims.claim: 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer was selected for subsequent experiments.
claims.source: As the improvements in cutting efficiency, while statistically significant, were only in the range of ~10% and both increased toxicity, we selected 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer for subsequent experiments.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the decision-making process based on experimental data.

claims.claim: Long ssODN donors showed a very low integration efficiency of 3% at 20 pmol and a high toxicity.
claims.source: While the long ssODN donors showed a very low integration efficiency of 3% at 20 pmol and a high toxicity, short ssODN donors were more promising with an integration rate of 12% at 50 pmol and a lesser though still appreciable toxicity (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E and F to support this claim about long ssODN performance.

claims.claim: Higher concentrations of short ssODN further raised efficiency though with a corresponding increase in toxicity beyond a usable range.
claims.source: Higher concentrations of short ssODN further raised efficiency though with a corresponding increase in toxicity beyond a usable range (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E and F to support this claim about dose-response effects.

claims.claim: The AAV donor at 400 MOI and short ssODN at 50 pmol are the most suitable donors.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that the AAV donor at 400 MOI and short ssODN at 50 pmol are the most suitable donors.
claims.evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing different donor types and concentrations.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in editing efficiency for AZD7648 at 0.5 and 5 µM.
claims.source: There was also no significant difference in editing efficiency for AZD7648 at 0.5 and 5 µM but a slight improvement in viability (FDR = 0.16 and FDR = 0.01, respectively Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis in Figure 2A and B to support this claim about AZD7648 dose effects.

claims.claim: Repeating tests on the SF3B1 locus revealed similar trends, though with a somewhat lower mean editing efficiency of 57%.
claims.source: Repeating these tests on the SF3B1 locus revealed similar trends, though with a somewhat lower mean editing efficiency of 57% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B to support this claim about locus-specific effects.

claims.claim: The lower efficiency at SF3B1 reflects the lower cutting efficiency observed at this locus.
claims.source: This difference reflects the lower cutting efficiency observed at this locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: The results section relates the editing efficiency to cutting efficiency data from earlier experiments.

claims.claim: Limiting the number of co-processed samples can substantially improve editing to near perfect efficiencies.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that limiting the number of co-processed samples, and the addition of 0.5 µM AZD7648 for the 48 hr following editing could substantially improve editing to near perfect efficiencies.
claims.evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the experimental data about factors affecting efficiency.

claims.claim: With the short ssODN, a mean editing efficiency of 44% was observed under optimal conditions.
claims.source: With the short ssODN, we observed a mean editing efficiency of 44% under these conditions, increased from the 13% but still substantially lower than AAV (Figure 2F and G), and consistent with reports for 53BP1 inhibition (De Ravin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G and cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim.

claims.claim: The difference between AAV and ssODN efficiency was likely due to the further disruption of the spacer sequence provided by the synthetic intron in the AAV donor.
claims.source: Further thought into the differences between the two suggested that perhaps it was the further disruption of the spacer sequence provided by the synthetic intron in the AAV donor which provided the difference (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on comparison of donor designs.

claims.claim: Some substitutions were present both in and around the predicted off-target regions, however, these were equivalent for a given individual between both edited conditions (+/-AZD7568) and unmanipulated controls.
claims.source: Some substitutions were present both in and around the predicted off-target regions, however, these were equivalent for a given individual between both edited conditions (+/-AZD7568) and unmanipulated controls (paired t-test FDRs >0.3, individual values in Supplementary file 1) indicating they were not introduced by the editing process.
claims.evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis to support this claim about background substitutions.

claims.claim: Phenotypes involving CD49f are not all stable on cultured cells.
claims.source: While phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019), not all of these markers are stable on cultured cells.
claims.evidence: The results section cites published literature and provides additional context about marker stability.

claims.claim: The panel used for sorting consisted of only culture-stable markers which retained the ability to sort sub-populations from across the hierarchy.
claims.source: As such, we used a panel consisting of only culture-stable markers which retained the ability to sort sub-populations from across the hierarchy.
claims.evidence: The results section describes the methodological approach based on marker stability considerations.

claims.claim: The decrease in advanced progenitor phenotype is consistent with the slight drop in colony number.
claims.source: This is consistent with the observed decrease in CFC frequency (Figure 3D), suggesting that later progenitors may be more affected by editing than the most primitive subsets.
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation connecting two experimental observations.

claims.claim: Overall editing efficiencies in the zygosity tuning tests were lower than normal due to the requirement of simultaneously editing many conditions.
claims.source: It should be noted that overall editing efficiencies in these tests were lower than normal due to the requirement of simultaneously editing many conditions.
claims.evidence: The results section provides context for the experimental results based on earlier observations about condition number effects.

claims.claim: The analysis of zygosity was not confounded by differential clonogenicity of specific mutational statuses.
claims.source: These results suggest that this analysis was not confounded by differential clonogenicity of specific mutational statuses (homozygous WT/silent, heterozygous, homozygous mutant).
claims.evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the clonogenic efficiency data.

claims.claim: Desired zygosity ratios could be predicted based on simple sampling calculations.
claims.source: Desired zygosity ratios could thus be predicted based on simple sampling calculations.
claims.evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the observed linear relationship between donor ratio and zygosity.

claims.claim: The current study demonstrates a near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPC.
claims.source: The current study demonstrates a near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPC and identifies the key design and technical considerations needed to achieve it.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the main finding of the study.

claims.claim: The current study identifies the key design and technical considerations needed to achieve near-perfect editing efficiency.
claims.source: The current study demonstrates a near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPC and identifies the key design and technical considerations needed to achieve it.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the main contribution of the study.

claims.claim: ssODN donors are much cheaper, faster to iterate, and more stable than AAV donors.
claims.source: This simple design change facilitates the use of these much cheaper, faster to iterate, and more stable donors.
claims.evidence: The discussion provides context about the advantages of ssODN donors based on general knowledge.

claims.claim: The handling time effect may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection.
claims.source: This likely corresponds to the handling time, and may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection previously reported (Charlesworth et al., 2018).

results.result: The study achieved mean precise editing efficiencies >90% in primary cord blood HSPCs through optimization of protocol components. Key modifications included addition of DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648 (0.5 µM), p53 siRNA, and incorporation of spacer-breaking silent mutations in ssODN donors in addition to PAM mutations. With AAV donors, mean efficiency reached 97%, while ssODN donors with spacer mutations achieved 94% efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C37, C40-C42 collectively demonstrate the achievement of >90% editing efficiency through specific protocol modifications. The data in Figures 2A-G show statistically significant improvements with AZD7648 and spacer mutations, with appropriate controls and multiple biological replicates across different cord blood donors. The statistical analyses (FDR corrections) and dose-response relationships support the conclusions.

results.result: AZD7648 was identified as superior to M3814 for improving HDR efficiency in HSPCs. At 0.5 µM, AZD7648 showed improved editing efficiency compared to M3814 and was equivalent to 5 µM M3814, while also demonstrating marginally but statistically significantly lower toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C34-C35, C56 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-B with appropriate statistical analysis (FDR values). The comparison between DNA-PK inhibitors is direct and controlled, with multiple biological replicates. The conclusion that AZD7648 is optimal is consistent with cited literature on its improved specificity (C33).

results.result: Editing efficiency was even across the hematopoietic progenitor hierarchy, including long-term HSCs, intermediate HSCs, multipotent/erythroid progenitors, and advanced progenitors. No significant differences in editing efficiencies were observed between phenotypically defined sub-populations and bulk measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C45, C61, C107 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A showing no significant differences across sorted populations. The use of culture-stable markers (C93) and appropriate statistical analysis strengthen this conclusion. However, the study did not perform in vivo transplantation to definitively confirm functional LT-HSC editing (acknowledged in C102).

results.result: Editing did not substantially distort the progenitor hierarchy, though a slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of CD34+ cells with advanced progenitor phenotype (FDR=0.007), consistent with decreased CFC frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46, C94 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B with appropriate statistical analysis. The interpretation connecting the decrease in advanced progenitors to CFC frequency (C94) is reasonable given the data in Figure 3D. The effect is modest and the authors appropriately characterize it as not substantially distorting the hierarchy.

results.result: Editing did not affect the distribution of lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays. No changes to colony type (GEMM, GM, E) were observed despite a quantitative decrease in total colony numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C49, C62 are supported by CFC assay data in Figure 3E showing equivalent proportions of colony types between edited and control cells. The data demonstrate that while total CFC numbers decreased (C47-C48), the differentiation capacity of remaining cells was preserved. Multiple biological replicates strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Editing did not affect the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells (LTC-ICs). No significant difference was observed in highly proliferative clone frequencies between edited and control cells, which correlate with HSCs having highest regenerative potential in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C51, C77 are supported by LTC-IC assay data in Figure 3I with appropriate statistical analysis using Extreme Limiting Dilution Analysis. The clonal assay provides functional assessment of stem cell capacity. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge (C102) that in vivo transplantation was not performed to definitively confirm functional LT-HSC preservation.

results.result: Overall editing efficiency and zygosity can be tuned by adding defined mixtures of mutant and wild-type (silent) donors. A highly significant monotonic relationship (p<<0.001) was observed between donor ratio and mutant allele frequency, with zygosity distribution predictable by simple sampling calculations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C53, C55, C97, C108 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B-D showing linear relationship between donor ratios and editing outcomes. The statistical analysis is appropriate and the clonogenic efficiency data (C54, C96) confirms the analysis was not confounded by differential survival of specific genotypes. This provides a practical method for disease modeling requiring heterozygosity.

results.result: No detectable off-target edits were observed at the top 3 predicted off-target sites, regardless of AZD7648 addition. Substitutions present in off-target regions were equivalent between edited conditions and unmanipulated controls, indicating they were not introduced by editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C67, C91, C106 are supported by nanopore sequencing data in Figure 2H and supplements with appropriate statistical analysis (paired t-tests, FDR>0.3). The analysis included three independent donors and appropriate controls. However, the analysis was limited to predicted off-target sites and did not include genome-wide assessment of potential off-target effects.

results.result: At lower RNP concentrations, electroporation enhancer provided slight benefit (FDR=0.02), but this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR=0.48). Increasing RNP concentration improved editing efficiency (FDR=0.08), but both modifications increased toxicity. Therefore, 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer was selected for subsequent experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26, C80-C81 are supported by T7E1 assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with appropriate statistical analysis. The decision to use 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer represents a reasonable balance between efficiency and toxicity. The ~10% improvement in efficiency was deemed insufficient to justify the toxicity increase.

results.result: AAV at 400 MOI achieved 19.8% integration efficiency prior to observable toxicity. Short ssODN donors showed 12% integration at 50 pmol with lesser toxicity, while long ssODN showed only 3% integration at 20 pmol with high toxicity. These concentrations (400 MOI AAV, 50 pmol short ssODN) were identified as most suitable.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C82-C84 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1C-F comparing different donor types and concentrations. The BspEI assay was validated to ~1% accuracy (C28). The conclusion about optimal concentrations is reasonable based on the efficiency-toxicity tradeoff, though the authors acknowledge some toxicity remains even at these concentrations.

results.result: Toxicity for ssODN donors was independent of Cas9 nuclease presence, suggesting it is likely mediated by innate immune responses to single-stranded DNA rather than the editing process itself. Much of the toxicity in cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery regardless of editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C65-C66 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing equivalent toxicity with and without RNP. The interpretation that toxicity is mediated by innate immune responses is reasonable and supported by cited literature (C66). However, this remains an inference rather than direct demonstration of immune pathway activation.

results.result: The addition of RS1 (RAD51 stabilizer) either alone or together with AZD7648 was detrimental to editing efficiency and toxic to cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing decreased efficiency and viability with RS1 addition. This negative result is important for protocol optimization, though the mechanism for the detrimental effect is not explored.

results.result: The number of conditions simultaneously processed at nucleofection had a substantial effect on editing efficiency, with a negative correlation observed (R²=0.55, p<<0.001). This likely corresponds to handling time and may be analogous to the AAV delivery window post-nucleofection.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C59-C60, C95 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2E showing correlation between condition number and efficiency. The statistical relationship is significant, though the R² of 0.55 indicates substantial unexplained variance. The interpretation about handling time is reasonable but remains speculative without direct measurement of timing effects.

results.result: A modest decrease in CFC potential was observed with editing, with colony numbers decreased even with donor alone and further decreased with editing. A non-significant trend toward decreased low proliferation LTC-IC suggests late progenitors may be more sensitive to editing than primitive subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C64, C103 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3D and 3I. The interpretation that late progenitors are more sensitive is reasonable given the pattern of effects, though the LTC-IC trend was not statistically significant (C52). The authors appropriately note that remaining CFCs retain normal function (C104).

results.result: Colonies from edited cells showed a preponderance of homozygous edits, as expected from the high editing efficiencies achieved.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing zygosity distribution in colonies. This result is consistent with the high overall editing efficiencies and provides single-cell validation of the bulk measurements.

results.result: A nested PCR approach was required to avoid non-specific amplification from non-integrated AAV donors. The BspEI-based assay for ssODN integration was validated to be accurate down to ~1% integration efficiency using defined DNA mixtures.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by methodological validation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B. These technical validations are important for ensuring accurate measurement of integration efficiency. The nested PCR approach addresses a critical technical challenge with AAV donor detection.

results.result: There was a non-significant trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation and transient clones in the edited condition.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 describes a trend that did not reach statistical significance in the LTC-IC assay (Figure 3I). While the authors note this trend is consistent with decreased CFC frequency, the lack of statistical significance means this observation requires further validation to determine if it represents a real biological effect.

results.result: No significant differences in clonogenic efficiency were observed across different donor ratio conditions in zygosity tuning experiments, suggesting the analysis was not confounded by differential clonogenicity of specific mutational statuses.
results.evaluation: Claims C54 and C96 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C. This control is important for validating that the zygosity tuning approach reflects true editing outcomes rather than selective survival of particular genotypes. However, the absence of large clones in the 100% mutant condition suggests some effect on highly proliferative cells.

results.result: Testing at the SF3B1 locus revealed similar trends to SRSF2, though with lower mean editing efficiency of 57%, which reflects the lower cutting efficiency observed at this locus. No significant difference in editing efficiency was observed for AZD7648 at 0.5 and 5 µM at SF3B1.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D. The locus-specific differences demonstrate that gRNA quality affects overall efficiency, but the protocol improvements are generalizable. The consistency of AZD7648 effects across loci strengthens the main conclusions.

results.result: Additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence were necessary to achieve maximal efficiencies with ssODN donors. The difference between AAV and ssODN efficiency was likely due to spacer disruption provided by the synthetic intron in AAV donors, which has been built-in to most AAV systems but not competing ssODN designs.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C90 represent interpretations supported by the experimental comparison between donor designs (Figure 2F-G) and cited literature. The dramatic improvement in ssODN efficiency with spacer mutations (from 44% to 94%) strongly supports this interpretation. The comparison to AAV donor designs is well-supported by citations.

results.result: During publication, another study (Selvaraj et al., 2024) reported similar effects of AZD7648 in HSPCs and other cell types, achieving similar efficiencies with AAV6 donors but slightly lower efficiencies with ssODN. The differences in ssODN efficiency are likely attributable to shorter donor length and choice of silent spacer mutations, both factors previously shown to impact integration efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 appropriately contextualize the current work relative to concurrent publication. The comparison is fair and the authors identify both similarities and differences. The interpretation of why ssODN efficiencies differ is supported by cited literature (C72) and the current study's findings. This cross-validation strengthens confidence in the main conclusions.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological and technical context for the study, including that NHEJ is the default DNA repair pathway, HDR operates only in S/G2 phase, typical HDR efficiencies in HSPCs are 10-20%, and various approaches including p53 knockdown, 53BP1 inhibition, and DNA-PK inhibition have been shown to improve efficiency while maintaining stem cell function.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C20 represent established knowledge from cited literature that provides appropriate context for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is accurate based on the cited sources. These claims establish the rationale for the current study's approach.

results.result: The culture protocol was based on established methods, including 48 hr pre-stimulation that induces primitive HSCs to cycle by ~66 hr, addition of UM171 to maintain HSC function and improve transduction, use of culture-stable markers for phenotyping, and maintenance of cell density below 250,000 cells/mL to prevent auto-inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C78-C79 describe methodological choices based on the authors' previous work and cited literature. These represent appropriate application of established methods. The citations to prior work (Knapp et al., 2017; Fares et al., 2014; Ngom et al., 2018) support these methodological choices.

results.result: The P95H mutation in SRSF2 introduced by the PAM mutation in mutant donors is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, and clonal hematopoiesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by cited literature (Watson et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2011; van der Werf et al., 2021). This contextualizes why silent donors were used for functional assays to isolate effects of the editing process from effects of the disease-associated mutation.

results.result: Previous reports demonstrated that editing rates were consistent pre- and post-transplantation with and without DNA-PK inhibition, and that NHEJ inhibition with donor present did not increase off-target editing or large-scale genomic rearrangements.
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C68 accurately represent findings from cited literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021). These prior findings provide important context for interpreting the safety and functional preservation observed in the current study.

results.result: While CD49f-based phenotypes are highly selective on fresh cells, not all markers are stable on cultured cells. Therefore, a panel of culture-stable markers was used that retained ability to sort sub-populations across the hierarchy.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 represent appropriate methodological considerations based on cited literature and practical constraints. The choice to use culture-stable markers is well-justified and the selected panel (CD34, CD45RA, CD90, CD49c) has been validated in prior work (Tomellini et al., 2019).

results.result: The study demonstrates near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPCs and identifies key design and technical considerations needed to achieve it.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 represent appropriate summary statements of the study's main contributions. The experimental data throughout the manuscript support these conclusions, with mean efficiencies of 97% for AAV and 94% for optimized ssODN donors achieved through specific protocol modifications.

results.result: ssODN donors are much cheaper, faster to iterate, and more stable than AAV donors.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 represents general knowledge about the practical advantages of synthetic oligonucleotides versus viral vector production. While not directly demonstrated in this study, this is widely accepted in the field and provides important context for why achieving high efficiency with ssODN donors is valuable.

results.result: It remains a formal possibility that functionally defined LT-HSCs may be edited at lower frequency or functionally compromised, though clonal LTC-IC data suggest this is not the case.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 appropriately acknowledges a limitation of the study - the lack of in vivo transplantation data. While the LTC-IC data (C51) and prior literature (C63) suggest functional LT-HSCs are preserved, definitive confirmation would require xenotransplantation experiments. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The authors propose that interference with innate immune pathways may mitigate toxicity, and that the protocol will enable disease modeling and improve therapeutic editing approaches currently in clinical trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C109-C110 represent forward-looking statements and speculation about future applications. While reasonable based on the study's findings, these represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. The potential applications are plausible but require future validation.

results.result: The authors achieved mean precise editing efficiencies >90% in primary cord blood HSPCs through protocol optimization, specifically by adding the DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648 (superior to M3814), incorporating spacer-breaking silent mutations in donors, combining with p53 siRNA, and limiting the number of simultaneously processed conditions. These modifications improved editing from baseline levels (~20%) to near-perfect efficiencies (up to 97% with AAV and 94% with optimized ssODN donors).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a major advance, stating 'the significant increase in HDR facilitated by the authors' described application of AZD7648 and the preservation of a pool of targeted progenitors is encouraging.' They note 'the sum of the adjustments to the editing procedure have yielded important advances towards minimizing editing toxicity while maximizing editing efficiency in HSPCs.' The evidence is described as 'convincing.'

results.result: The authors found no detectable off-target edits at the top 3 predicted off-target sites, either with or without AZD7648, suggesting the protocol does not substantially increase off-target editing frequencies. This is consistent with previous studies using 53BP1 inhibition showing no increases in off-target editing when donor was present.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the evidence supporting the claims is convincing in that primitive LTC-ICs were minimally affected as a result of the editing procedure and the lack of edits at predicted off-target sites.' This safety finding is treated as important supporting evidence for the methodology.

results.result: Editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy, with no significant differences in editing efficiencies observed across phenotypically defined sub-populations including HSC, intermediate HSC, multipotent progenitors, and advanced progenitors. The editing process and addition of AZD7648 did not preferentially affect specific hierarchical levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding, noting the authors 'show that the editing process and addition of AZD7648 edits evenly across the HSPC hierarchy.' One reviewer specifically highlights this as a unique contribution 'beyond what was done in the other manuscript,' indicating acceptance of the claim.

results.result: Editing did not substantially distort the progenitor hierarchy, with generally equivalent representation of each population within the CD34 compartment between edited and control cells, though a slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of advanced progenitor phenotype cells (FDR = 0.007).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the evidence that 'the editing process and addition of AZD7648...does not substantially affect the distribution of progenitor phenotypes.' The slight decrease in advanced progenitors is acknowledged but not challenged, consistent with the overall conclusion of minimal hierarchy distortion.

results.result: Editing did not affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell (CFC) assays, with no changes to colony type distribution observed despite a quantitative drop in total colony numbers. The distribution of myeloid outputs (GEMM, GM, E colonies) remained unchanged, suggesting remaining progenitors retained normal differentiation capacity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding, noting the authors 'similarly show that CFC distributions are not affected by the editing process' and that this demonstrates 'the preservation of a pool of targeted progenitors.' The evidence is described as 'convincing' that 'functional progenitors can be successfully edited.'

results.result: Editing did not affect the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells (LTC-ICs), with no significant difference in highly proliferative clone frequencies between edited cells and non-edited controls. This suggests the editing process does not substantially affect the most regenerative subset of HSCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the evidence supporting the claims is convincing in that primitive LTC-ICs were minimally affected as a result of the editing procedure.' They further note the authors show the protocol 'critically does not affect the LTC-ICs with the highest self-renewal potential,' treating this as a key finding supporting functional preservation.

results.result: A modest decrease in colony-forming cell (CFC) potential was observed with editing, with colony numbers dropping approximately 4-fold. A slight drop in colony number was observed even without editing (consistent with donor-induced toxicity), which was further decreased with editing. There was also a non-significant trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation LTC-ICs, suggesting late progenitors may be more sensitive to the editing process than the most primitive subsets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge, noting 'the preservation of a pool of targeted progenitors' despite the quantitative decrease. They accept the authors' interpretation that 'remaining CFCs appear to retain normal function' and treat the modest toxicity as an acknowledged limitation rather than a fundamental flaw in the methodology.

results.result: Overall editing and zygosity can be tuned by adding defined mixtures of mutant and wild-type (silent) donors, with a highly significant monotonic decrease in mutant allele frequency observed with increasing silent donor proportion (p<<0.001). A preponderance of homozygous edits was observed with all mutant donors, with progressive increase in heterozygous or homozygous silent edits as silent donor proportion increased. Desired zygosity ratios could be predicted based on simple sampling calculations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the ability to zygosity tune was convincingly presented and provides a valuable strategy to modify this HDR procedure towards more accurate disease modelling.' They treat this as a unique and important contribution of the study for mutation modeling applications.

results.result: Additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence (beyond PAM disruption) were necessary to achieve maximal editing efficiencies with ssODN donors. The incorporation of spacer-breaking mutations drastically improved ssODN editing efficiency from 44% to 94%, nearly matching AAV performance. Even designs with only silent spacer mutations but no PAM mutation achieved 84% efficiency, highlighting the critical importance of spacer disruption in donor design.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight 'the discovery of the effectiveness of spacer breaking changes in ssODNs allowing for substantially increased targeting efficiency is a promising advance towards democratizing these editing strategies given the ease of designing and synthesizing ssODNs relative to the production of viral donors.' This is treated as a significant methodological contribution.

results.result: The number of conditions simultaneously processed at the time of nucleofection had a substantial effect on editing efficiency, with a negative correlation observed between condition number and efficiency (R²=0.55). This likely corresponds to handling time and may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection. Technical factors associated with cell handling and nucleofection timing play an important role in overall efficiency.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding, noting the authors 'provided useful insights into optimizing the practicalities of the experimental procedures that will aid bench scientists in effectively carrying out these editing approaches, for example avoiding longer handling times inherent when scaling up to editing over multiple conditions.' This practical insight is valued as a methodological contribution.

results.result: Toxicity for ssODN donors was independent of the presence of Cas9 nuclease (equivalent in the no RNP condition), suggesting it is likely an innate immune reaction to single-stranded DNA rather than the editing process itself. Much of the toxicity in both direct cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery regardless of editing, likely mediated by innate immune responses to DNA.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this interpretation and accept the authors' characterization of toxicity sources. The finding is treated as part of the overall assessment that the protocol achieves 'important advances towards minimizing editing toxicity while maximizing editing efficiency,' implicitly accepting the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: It remains a formal possibility that functionally defined long-term HSCs may either be edited at lower frequency or functionally compromised, though the authors' clonal LTC-IC data would suggest this is not the case. The authors acknowledge they did not perform in vivo xenotransplantation experiments to directly assess long-term engraftment potential.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this limitation, stating 'as the authors acknowledge it remains to be verified to what degree the survival/self-renewal capacity and in vivo regenerative potential of the more primitive fractions is maintained with their strategy.' However, they note 'the inclusion of LTC-IC assays that verify the lack of effect on these quite primitive cells is encouraging that functionality of stem cells will be similarly spared,' indicating the evidence is suggestive but not definitive.

results.result: At lower RNP concentrations, there was a slight benefit from adding an electroporation enhancer (FDR = 0.02), though this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR = 0.48). Increasing RNP concentration showed a benefit to overall editing efficiency (FDR = 0.08), but both the electroporation enhancer and increased RNP concentration resulted in significantly decreased cell numbers indicating toxicity. The authors selected 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer for subsequent experiments as the optimal balance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these optimization findings and implicitly accept them as part of the methodological development. The findings are treated as supporting the overall conclusion that the authors achieved 'important advances towards minimizing editing toxicity while maximizing editing efficiency.'

results.result: For AAV donors, 400 MOI gave the highest integration rate prior to observable toxicity (19.8%). For ssODN donors, short ssODNs (90 bp) showed 12% integration at 50 pmol with lesser toxicity, while long ssODNs (200 bp) showed very low integration (3% at 20 pmol) with high toxicity. Higher concentrations of short ssODN further raised efficiency but with toxicity beyond a usable range. The authors concluded AAV at 400 MOI and short ssODN at 50 pmol are the most suitable donors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these donor optimization findings. The systematic comparison is implicitly accepted as part of the methodological rigor, with reviewers noting 'the methods are clearly described and the experiments for the most part also appropriately powered.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the achievement of >90% editing efficiency through protocol modifications (C1-C3, C37, C40-C42). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and dose-response relationships, while peer reviewers highlight this as a 'major advance' with 'convincing' evidence. Peer review also includes DNA-PK inhibitor claims (C32, C34-C35, C56) in their evaluation.

Both support the DNA-PK inhibitor optimization claims (C32, C34-C35, C56). OpenEval treats this as a separate finding with focus on AZD7648's optimal performance, while peer reviewers group it with overall efficiency achievements as part of the major methodological advance.

Perfect agreement on claims C4, C45, C61, C107 regarding even editing across HSPC hierarchy. Both acknowledge the lack of in vivo transplantation data as a limitation. Peer reviewers specifically highlight this as a unique contribution 'beyond what was done in the other manuscript.'

Both support the finding of modest decrease in advanced progenitors (C5, C46). OpenEval includes C94 connecting this to CFC frequency, while peer review includes C61 (hierarchy preservation). Both characterize the effect as not substantially distorting the hierarchy.

Both support preserved differentiation capacity in CFC assays (C6, C49, C62). OpenEval emphasizes equivalent colony type proportions despite decreased total numbers. Peer reviewers include C74 and describe evidence as 'convincing' that 'functional progenitors can be successfully edited.'

Both support LTC-IC preservation claims (C7, C51). OpenEval includes C77 and emphasizes statistical analysis methodology. Peer reviewers include C107 and explicitly state evidence is 'convincing' that 'primitive LTC-ICs were minimally affected,' treating this as a key finding.

Perfect agreement on zygosity tuning capability (C8, C53, C55, C97, C108). Both treat this as an important methodological contribution. Peer reviewers explicitly state it was 'convincingly presented and provides a valuable strategy' for disease modeling.

Both support off-target safety findings (C43-C44, C67, C106). OpenEval notes the limitation to predicted sites without genome-wide assessment. Peer reviewers include C68 and explicitly state evidence is 'convincing' regarding 'lack of edits at predicted off-target sites.'

Perfect agreement on toxicity mechanism interpretation (C31, C65-C66). Both support the conclusion that toxicity is mediated by innate immune responses rather than RNP. OpenEval notes this remains an inference; peer reviewers accept without challenge.

Both support the correlation between handling time and efficiency (C38-C39, C59-C60). OpenEval includes C95 and notes R²=0.55 indicates substantial unexplained variance. Peer reviewers explicitly value this as 'useful insights into optimizing practicalities' for bench scientists.

Perfect agreement on differential toxicity effects (C47-C48, C64, C103). Both support the interpretation that late progenitors are more sensitive. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'preservation of a pool of targeted progenitors' despite quantitative decrease.

Both strongly support the spacer mutation breakthrough for ssODN efficiency (C57-C58, C90). OpenEval emphasizes the dramatic improvement (44% to 94%). Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'a promising advance towards democratizing these editing strategies.'
